business.what_it_does: Fathom is a Google Analytics alternative that makes your analytics easy to understand and respects visitor privacy, tracking website pageviews and traffic sources via a single embed script without cookies.
business.business_model: subscription, priced by monthly pageviews across all sites on an account, billed monthly or yearly

facts.statement: Fathom is a Google Analytics alternative that makes your analytics easy to understand and respects visitor privacy.

provenance.quote: Fathom is a Google Analytics alternative that makes your analytics easy to understand and respects visitor privacy.

facts.statement: Fathom doesn't use cookies, so sites can keep analytics without a consent/cookie banner.

provenance.quote: You don’t need a consent banner that annoys visitors, clutters your layout and slows the page down. Fathom doesn’t use cookies, so you can keep analytics on your site without the pop-up.

facts.statement: EU isolation is enabled by default for every customer on every plan; EU visitor data is processed in the EU and all other visitor data is processed in the US.

provenance.quote: as a Fathom customer, you’re already using it, and it’s enabled by default! ... Fathom automatically and intelligently routes data from EU visitors to be processed in the EU and all other visitors to be processed in the US.

facts.statement: Customers who need all global traffic routed through the EU can switch to the EU CDN endpoint for Extreme EU Isolation.

provenance.quote: If you need to use Extreme EU Isolation, where all global traffic is routed through the EU, please use `https://cdn-eu.usefathom.com/script.js` instead.

facts.statement: Pageviews blocked via the site firewall (pages, IPs, domains, countries) do not count against a plan's pageview allotment.

provenance.quote: Visitors who visit blocked pages do not count as pageviews, so they do not count against your payment plan allotment of pageviews.

facts.statement: Every plan includes at least 50 sites, with bigger plans including more, and up to 15 extra packs of 50 sites can be added for $10/month or $100/year per pack.

provenance.quote: Every plan includes at least 50 sites, and bigger plans include more. Select a plan above to see exactly how many. If you need more, you can add up to 15 packs of 50 extra sites yourself from your billing settings, at $10/month or $100/year per pack.

facts.statement: GA4 historical data can be imported into Fathom at no extra charge, and imported history remains viewable and exportable while the subscription is active.

provenance.quote: We don’t charge extra for historical imports. Your imported history stays available to view and export while your Fathom subscription is active.

facts.statement: Fathom does not offer sales calls or live demos; prospective customers evaluate the product via a recorded walkthrough, the live demo dashboard, documentation, or a trial.

provenance.quote: We don’t do sales calls or live demos, but our software is ridiculously easy to use. You can watch our 10-minute walkthrough, click around the live dashboard or give Fathom a 7-day free trial alongside your existing analytics.

facts.statement: Fathom does not offer a free plan; its stated reasoning is that its business model is selling software, not visitor data.

provenance.quote: Nope, and here’s why: we’ve invested heavily in fast, reliable infrastructure (we don’t host Fathom on cheap servers that go offline). Our business model is selling software, not your data, so we’ve priced Fathom to be sustainable for a very long time.

facts.statement: Fathom adjusts customers between plan tiers based on two consecutive months of pageview usage, rather than changing mid-cycle for a single spike.

provenance.quote: Of course! If you exceed your limit for two months in a row, we’ll get in touch about a larger plan. Or, if you’re under your current tier for two months in a row (and it’s not our lowest tier already), you can move to a smaller plan from your billing settings.

facts.statement: Fathom primarily targets businesses currently on Google Analytics (including GA4) who want a privacy-focused, cookieless replacement without losing their historical data.
Pricing is account-wide and pageview-based across all sites on the account, not charged per individual site.

entries.claim: EU isolation is enabled by default for every Fathom customer, with nothing to set up.
entries.verbatim: If you want to use [EU isolation](https://usefathom.com/features/data-isolation), congratulations; as a Fathom customer, you’re already using it, and it’s enabled by default!

entries.claim: No changes to the embed script are needed to use EU isolation.
entries.verbatim: There’s nothing you have to set up or tweak or even change in [your embed script](/docs/script/embed) to use it. Fathom automatically and intelligently routes data from EU visitors to be processed in the EU and all other visitors to be processed in the US.

entries.claim: Fathom automatically routes data from EU visitors to be processed in the EU, and data from all other visitors to be processed in the US.
entries.verbatim: There’s nothing you have to set up or tweak or even change in [your embed script](/docs/script/embed) to use it. Fathom automatically and intelligently routes data from EU visitors to be processed in the EU and all other visitors to be processed in the US.

entries.claim: EU isolation treats visitors from Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland, and the United Kingdom as EU for data-routing purposes, even though they are non-EU member nations.
entries.verbatim: It includes visitors from the following non-eu member nations: - Iceland - Liechtenstein - Norway - Switzerland - United Kingdom

context.subject: Fathom Analytics - EU isolation
context.conditions: applies to visitor data-routing classification under EU isolation

entries.claim: Fathom's EU servers are located in Falkenstein, Helsinki, and Nuremberg.
entries.verbatim: - Falkenstein - Helsinki - Nuremberg

entries.claim: Extreme EU Isolation routes all global traffic through the EU by using the script URL https://cdn-eu.usefathom.com/script.js instead of the default embed script.
entries.verbatim: If you need to use Extreme EU Isolation, where all global traffic is routed through the EU, please use `https://cdn-eu.usefathom.com/script.js` instead.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics - Extreme EU Isolation
context.conditions: requires using the cdn-eu.usefathom.com script URL instead of the default one

entries.claim: Firewall settings are adjusted by going to Settings, then Sites, clicking the site, then clicking the Firewall tab.
entries.verbatim: To adjust your firewall settings, go to `Settings`, then `Sites`, click on your site, then click the `Firewall` tab.

entries.claim: The site firewall offers six list tabs to configure: Pages, IPs, Referrers, Domains, Countries, and Events.
entries.verbatim: Open a list tab (Pages, IPs, Referrers, Domains, Countries, or Events).

entries.claim: Blocking pages, IPs, domains, or countries in the firewall does not restrict visitor access to the site; it only prevents those visits from appearing in the Fathom dashboard.
entries.verbatim: Note: If you've blocked pages, IPs, domains, or countries, visitors coming from those sources will still be able to access and navigate around your site, but their visits just won't be shown as data in your Fathom dashboard.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics - Site firewall (Pages/IPs/Domains/Countries blocking)
context.limitations: blocking hides data from the dashboard but does not restrict site access

entries.claim: Page blocking supports wildcards, such as /about/*, to block all pages under a given path (e.g. /about/team, /about/luna).
entries.verbatim: If you wanted to block all the pages under the `/about` page, so pages like `/about/team` and `/about/luna` and so on, you’d add a wildcard: ``` /about/* ```

context.subject: Fathom Analytics - Site firewall Pages blocking

entries.claim: Pageviews on blocked pages do not count as pageviews, so they do not count against the payment plan's pageview allotment.
entries.verbatim: Visitors who visit blocked pages do not count as pageviews, so they do not count against your payment plan allotment of pageviews.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics - Site firewall Pages blocking
context.conditions: applies to pageviews on blocked pages

entries.claim: IP blocking supports wildcard patterns, e.g. 100.100.100.* blocks any IP starting with 100.100.100., such as 100.100.100.1 and 100.100.100.123.
entries.verbatim: That means anyone with an IP address that started with `100.100.100.` would be blocked. So `100.100.100.1`, `100.100.100.123`, etc, would all be blocked.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics - Site firewall IP blocking

entries.claim: Only IPv4 addresses are currently supported for wildcard IP blocking.
entries.verbatim: **Note:** Currently only IPv4 addresses are supported for wildcards

context.subject: Fathom Analytics - Site firewall IP blocking
context.limitations: wildcard IP blocking does not support IPv6

entries.claim: Blocking a country in the firewall keeps that country's visitors able to view the website while excluding their pageviews and analytics data from showing up in Fathom.
entries.verbatim: Say you’re getting a ton of traffic from a country that your business doesn’t serve; add that country to the list. They’ll still be able to see your website, but their page views and analytics data won’t show up in Fathom.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics - Site firewall Countries blocking

entries.claim: Referrer blocking supports wildcards, e.g. *.example.com blocks all subdomains of example.com as referrers.
entries.verbatim: You can also use wildcards to block a group of referrers. For example, to block all subdomains of `example.com`, you would add: ``` *.example.com ```

context.subject: Fathom Analytics - Site firewall Referrers blocking

entries.claim: Once one or more allowed domains are added to the Domains firewall list, data coming from any other domain is blocked instantly.
entries.verbatim: **Once you add one or more allowed domains, this means data coming from any other domain will be blocked instantly**.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics - Site firewall Domains allow list

entries.claim: Wildcard domain entries like *.example.com in the allowed domains list cover subdomains (e.g. subdomain.example.com, www.example.com) but do not allow the root domain example.com itself.
entries.verbatim: We support wildcards here too, so if you want to allow all subdomains, you can use: ``` *.example.com ``` This then allows only subdomains of example.com, so: `subdomain.example.com` and `www.example.com`, etc. But note: using `*.example.com` would not allow `example.com`, so be careful.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics - Site firewall Domains allow list
context.limitations: *.example.com allows subdomains only, not the bare root domain

entries.claim: The Events firewall tab can drop junk/unwanted event names at collect time, or restrict collection to only the names sent on purpose.
entries.verbatim: Use the `Events` tab to drop junk or unwanted event names at collect time, or to collect only the names you send on purpose.

entries.claim: In the Events firewall, Block mode drops the listed event names while still collecting every other event; Allow mode collects only the listed names/wildcard patterns, and an empty allow list collects every event.
entries.verbatim: **Block** drops those names and still collects every other event. **Allow** collects only the names (and wildcard patterns) on the list. An empty allow list collects every event.

entries.claim: For dynamic event names (for example Shopify product titles), an Events allow list needs a wildcard such as 'Product *'; a tight allow list of exact names will drop those dynamic events.
entries.verbatim: If you send dynamic names (for example Shopify product titles), use a wildcard such as `Product *` on an allow list. A tight allow list of exact names will drop those dynamic events.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics - Site firewall Events (dynamic event names, e.g. Shopify)
context.conditions: example given is Shopify product titles as a dynamic event name source

entries.claim: The firewall only stops future visits; existing spam already in reports must be cleaned up using Data removals in the site's Manage settings.
entries.verbatim: The firewall stops future visits. To clean up spam that’s already in your reports, use `Data removals` in your site’s `Manage` settings.

entries.claim: Fathom's tracking script can be installed via Fathom's WordPress plugin or one of Fathom's other integrations, placed in the header of the site's code.
entries.verbatim: To start collecting data from your website, you need to [install our script](/docs/script/embed) in the header of your site’s code via our [WordPress plugin](/docs/integrations/wordpress) or using [one of our integrations](/docs/integrations)).

entries.claim: Fathom's dashboard is live and real-time, so script installation can be verified by checking whether a visit shows up in the 'Realtime' count at the top of the dashboard.
entries.verbatim: Fathom’s dashboard is live and real-time, so the best way to check if our script is installed is by visiting your website and seeing if your visit shows up in the “Realtime” count at the top of your dashboard.

entries.claim: Fathom provides a browser console command, fathom.blockTrackingForMe(), that blocks tracking for the current browser on a page where Fathom is installed.
entries.verbatim: If you only need to block tracking in your current browser, open your browser console on a page where Fathom is installed and run: ``` fathom.blockTrackingForMe(); ```

entries.claim: The blockTrackingForMe setting is stored in the browser's local storage, so it continues working for future visits from that browser.
entries.verbatim: This stores the setting in your browser’s local storage, so it will keep working for future visits from that browser.

entries.claim: Excluding local, staging, or test environment visits from Fathom also prevents those non-live pageviews from counting against the plan quota.
entries.verbatim: This also prevents non-live pageviews from counting against your plan quota.

context.subject: Fathom Analytics - plan quota
context.conditions: applies when local/staging/test environments are excluded via firewall or tracking-block methods

entries.claim: Fathom's embed script is a single script tag, <script src="https://cdn.usefathom.com/script.js" data-site="ABCDEFG" defer></script>, with the Site ID as the data-site attribute.
entries.verbatim: <script src="https://cdn.usefathom.com/script.js" data-site="ABCDEFG" defer></script>

context.subject: Fathom Analytics embed script
context.conditions: ABCDEFG is a placeholder for the actual Site ID

entries.claim: The Site ID is a short, unique code that identifies the site, needed for the tracking snippet, integrations, and API calls.
entries.verbatim: Your Site ID is a short, unique code that identifies your site. You’ll need it for your tracking snippet, integrations, and API calls.

entries.claim: Fathom's advanced script settings support ignoring canonicals, honouring DNT (Do Not Track), and single-page applications (SPAs), among other options.
entries.verbatim: See [advanced script settings](/docs/script/script-advanced) to learn more about ignoring canonicals, honouring DNT, SPAs and more.

entries.claim: Data Isolation is enabled by default for every Fathom customer on every plan.
entries.verbatim: If you’re a Fathom customer, then congratulations, you’re already using Data Isolation and complying with privacy laws! We enable this by default for everyone on every plan.

entries.claim: Every Fathom plan, including the smallest, includes Data Isolation, enabled by default.
entries.verbatim: Yes. Every plan includes Data Isolation, including the smallest. It’s enabled by default.

entries.claim: Fathom Analytics guarantees that a visit is anonymized and not used against the visitor, unlike websites that retain raw logs.
entries.verbatim: Whenever you visit a website, your IP address and User-Agent are sent to that website's servers (that's just how the internet works). Some websites retain raw logs of that information, keeping tabs on what you're browsing. Whilst others (i.e Fathom Analytics) guarantee that your visit is anonymized and not used against you.

entries.claim: Fathom's Data Isolation method works by intelligently routing visitors to the right place to process their data.
entries.verbatim: Fathom’s Data Isolation method works by intelligently routing visitors to the right place to process their data.

entries.claim: For visitors outside the EU, Fathom's EU-owned CDN Bunny.net sends the pageview to Fathom's US servers directly and anonymizes the IP address there.
entries.verbatim: **If a visitor is outside the EU**, our EU-owned CDN (Bunny.net) sends their pageview to our US servers directly and anonymizes their "data" (IP address).

context.subject: Bunny.net CDN (Fathom infrastructure)
context.conditions: visitor is outside the EU

entries.claim: For visitors inside the EU, Fathom's CDN routes the pageview to European servers that strip the IP address before it reaches US infrastructure, and the resulting anonymous data is stored on US servers with zero personal data attached.
entries.verbatim: **If a visitor is inside the EU**, our CDN sends their pageview to our European servers and anonymizes their data immediately. The IP address (personal data under GDPR) is stripped from the request inside of the EU and never reaches our US infrastructure. The anonymous data is then stored on our main US servers for fast and easy retrieval on our customer dashboards, but there’s zero personal data associated with any of it.

context.subject: Fathom Data Isolation
context.conditions: visitor is inside the EU

segments.name: A bootstrapped software founder who checks his own traffic and gave up on GA4 months ago
segments.situation: He owns one or two web properties he built himself — a marketing site, docs, a blog — and he is the only person who ever looks at the numbers. GA4 is installed because it always was. Opening it means a property picker, then reports laid out for a media team: sessions versus engaged sessions, event parameters, explore panels he has never configured. Customers in this position describe the comparison in their own words: one says Fathom is "such a pleasure to use compared to Google Analytics" with "just the right number of features", another calls it "a breath of fresh air" that "really gives you all the traffic metrics you could need". What he actually wants to know is small and recurring: did yesterday's launch post send anyone, is the pricing page being read, did that podcast mention do anything. Where he is likely working from (inferred, not observed): the week around a release, with changelog, support and shipping all on him, so anything that needs a weekly ritual to produce an answer simply does not get done — one customer reports that only after switching did he become "more attentive to my sites". If he is carrying a consent banner for analytics at all, it is likely one he pasted in once and has not revisited.

situation_provenance.quote: Analytics for Huberman Lab are solely powered by Fathom. It's such a pleasure to use compared to Google Analytics. There's just the right number of features, and their platform is incredibly intuitive.
Wow, what a breath of fresh air. I love how simple Fathom Analytics is, and it really gives you all the traffic metrics you could need.

segments.job_to_be_done: Know at a glance whether the thing he shipped this week landed, without reading the numbers becoming another job on the list.
segments.trigger: A launch day or a sudden spike — an HN front page, a newsletter mention, a podcast drop — when he wants to see what is happening right now and the tool he has either shows nothing yet or shows numbers he cannot interpret. objections.objection: Google Analytics is free and already installed. Paying $15/month to get less data is a hard sell to myself, let alone to a finance approver.
objections.answer: The evidence answers the 'why pay' with a business-model argument and a usability argument, not a cheaper price. Fathom states it sells software, not data, and names that as why rivals can be free (E161, E256, E201, E242); it explicitly refuses a free plan and says why (E200). On value: one single-page dashboard that does not need months of training (E68, E98), real-time data instead of 24–48 hours (E141), no consent banner because there are no cookies (E138, E222), every feature on every plan including 50 sites (E176, E178, E149), and history kept for as long as you subscribe (E224, E246, E180). Customer voices carry the switch decision better than the price argument does (E211, E202, E203). Nothing in the evidence reduces the price or offers a free tier, so the copy must win this on 'what GA4 costs you in time and in visitor trust', never on cost.

objections.objection: This will give me strictly less than GA4. No funnels, no path analysis, no audience segments, no cohort or demographic reports — the moment someone asks a real question I'll be stuck.
objections.answer: Only partly answerable, and the gap is real. The evidence enumerates exactly what the dashboard covers — live visitors, total visitors, pageviews, top pages, referrers, countries, devices, browsers, events, UTM campaigns (E99) — plus filters and saved views (E142, E143, E183), date comparisons and milestones (E145, E144), events with monetary value and currency (E146, E221, E181), UTM campaign reporting (E147, E182), Search Console terms and positions (E153), CSV export and an API on every plan (E151, E185). Fathom frames the narrowness as deliberate: a single page of data versus Matomo's 12 sections and 70+ reports (E98, E97), and a customer says there are 'just the right number of features' (E211) and 'all the traffic metrics you could need' (E202). But nothing in the ledger supports funnels, path/flow analysis, user segments, cohorts or demographics, and the GA4 importer explicitly does not recreate every GA4 report or import events (E62). For a reader who genuinely runs funnel analysis, this objection stands unanswered and should be met by naming the trade honestly, not by implying parity.

objections.objection: Switching means abandoning years of history and running two tools in parallel while I check the numbers agree. That is work I don't have time for.
objections.answer: Well answered, with caveats to state up front. Supported GA4 data imports into the Fathom dashboard (E56, E152, E240) at no extra charge (E57), stays viewable and exportable while the subscription is active (E58), and the process is authorise-with-a-button, pick sites, run (E96) — contrasted with Matomo's Google Cloud API-key route (E95). Fathom can run alongside existing analytics during the trial (E239, E193, E198), and install is one script tag or a pre-built integration (E225, E27, E154, E241, E22) verified by watching Realtime (E23). The caveats must be said out loud or they become a support ticket: daily-level supported data only, no GA events, not every report recreated (E62); filtering options and totals differ between the tools (E63); large imports may need smaller date ranges (E64); Universal Analytics data is gone because Google deleted it in July 2024 (E65, E94).

objections.objection: Our legal team will not accept a vendor's own word that it is GDPR compliant. Where is the audit, the DPA, the certification?
objections.answer: Partly answered, and the missing piece is the important one. What exists: EU isolation on by default for every customer on every plan with nothing to configure (E1, E2, E31, E42, E43, E89); the mechanics are documented — EU visitor IPs stripped inside the EU and never reaching US infrastructure, anonymised data stored in the US (E47, E30, E40), named EU server locations (E5), Iceland/Liechtenstein/Norway/Switzerland/UK treated as EU (E4), an Extreme EU Isolation endpoint for routing all global traffic through the EU (E6); Canadian corporation covered by Canada's EU adequacy decision (E213); controller/processor roles described (E87, E88); anonymisation via hashes and salts, no individual tracking (E162, E109, E110, E112, E113); no cookies ever (E111, E107, E67); compliance claimed across GDPR, ePrivacy, PECR, CCPA with privacy lawyers said to have vetted collection and storage (E139, E214, E254); Data Isolation built with EU legal experts (E31 context). What does not exist anywhere in the evidence: a named auditor, certifying body, certification scheme, or a DPA document — the compliance claims are explicitly self-declared (E39 notes no certifying body or audit named). For a buyer whose blocker is third-party attestation, this cannot be beaten with what we currently know.

objections.objection: My site gets a few thousand visits a month. The cheapest plan bills me for 100,000 pageviews I will never use, so I'm paying a premium to be a small customer.
objections.answer: Nothing in the evidence answers this. There is no free plan and the stated reason is infrastructure investment and a software-not-data business model (E200, E201); the lowest tier is $15/month for up to 100,000 monthly pageviews (E164, E175, E251); and the downgrade mechanism explicitly does not apply from the lowest tier (E196). The only offsetting facts are that the small plan carries the identical feature set (E176) and includes 50 sites with a shared account-wide allowance (E178, E149, E245, E191), which helps a reader with many small sites and does nothing for a reader with one. Treat this as a segment to exclude rather than an objection to answer.

objections.objection: Pageview-metered pricing punishes me for a good month. One viral post or a bot flood and I'm force-upgraded or cut off mid-campaign.
objections.answer: Strongly answered. Occasional spikes are never charged for and never switch analytics off (E195, E248); tier moves happen only after two consecutive months over or under the threshold, with an email and a choice rather than an automatic charge (E196); before any pause of dashboard and API access there are several reminders and extra time, and data keeps being collected throughout (E195, E249); bots, crawlers and DDoS junk are filtered automatically on every plan (E140, E184); firewall-blocked pages, IPs, domains and countries do not count against the allotment (E11, E9, E14), and excluded local/staging traffic does not either (E26); cancellation is self-serve with no contracts (E194, E61). The honest edge: custom events and API events also consume the pageview allowance (E192, E191), so an event-heavy implementation can rise a tier for reasons unrelated to traffic.

objections.objection: Seven days with a card on file, and you won't even get on a call. I can't evaluate a replacement for our analytics stack that fast.
objections.answer: Partly answered. Evaluation without signing up is explicitly provided for: a recorded walkthrough of about 8–10 minutes (E100, E198), a live demo dashboard anyone can click around (E198), every feature documented (E199), and email contact for specific questions (E199, E187). The trial can be run alongside existing analytics so nothing has to be torn out to test it (E193, E239, E198); the card is not charged until the trial ends and an email arrives before billing starts (E177, E193); cancellation is self-serve, contract-free, with export first (E194, E92). What is not answerable: there are no sales calls or live demos at all, by policy (E197), and no evidence supports extending the 7 days or a card-free trial. An enterprise buyer who needs a human on a call will not get one, and the copy should route them to the demo dashboard and docs instead of pretending otherwise.

objections.objection: Our acquisition stack is Google. GA4 feeds Google Ads conversions, our reporting lives in Looker Studio, and our agency works in GA4. Ripping it out breaks the paid side of the business.
objections.answer: Largely unanswered. The evidence supports campaign-level measurement via UTM tags with filtering by campaign to see traffic, pages and completed events (E147, E220, E182), events with monetary value and currency so sales totals sit next to completion counts (E146, E221, E181), Search Console connected for terms, clicks, impressions and positions (E153), and CSV export plus an API to move data into other tools (E151, E185, E71). There is nothing in the ledger about Google Ads conversion import, offline conversion upload, Looker Studio connectors, server-side tagging or Google Tag Manager, and nothing about multi-touch attribution. For a paid-acquisition team this objection cannot be beaten with current evidence; the realistic framing is Fathom alongside GA4 for the reporting humans read, not as a replacement for the ads plumbing.

objections.objection: Cookieless numbers won't match GA4. When traffic looks different on the new tool, I'm the one who has to explain the discrepancy to my boss or my client.
objections.answer: Half answered, and honestly so. Fathom itself states that imported data has different filtering options and that totals can differ between tools (E63) — useful for setting expectations before anyone is surprised. The directional argument is that the difference is in Fathom's favour: bots, crawlers and DDoS junk are filtered out so the dashboard shows people who actually visited (E140, E184), while cookie-based tools miss real people to blockers, cookies and sampling (E215), and individuals are never tracked, data being anonymised with hashes and salts (E162). Running both in parallel during the trial is explicitly supported, which is the only way to pre-empt the conversation (E239, E193). What is missing: no benchmark, study or measured comparison of Fathom's counts against GA4's exists in the evidence, so no figure can be promised.

objections.objection: I could self-host an open-source tracker or just use Cloudflare's free analytics. Why rent this?
objections.answer: Partly answered, and one part works against us. Fathom offers no self-hosted option at all — it is a hosted product by design so pageviews can be processed on a global CDN with EU data handled in the EU (E160). So a reader whose requirement is 'runs on my own box' has no answer here. Against open-source self-hosting, the evidence argues operational cost: Matomo's privacy features need setup and knowledge to be used correctly (E86), its import needs a Google Cloud API key and is complex for non-developers (E95), its script is 20KB or 50KB with more features and needs your own CDN to load fast worldwide (E104, E105), and hosted Matomo retains data only up to 24 months (E90) versus retention for as long as you remain a customer (E91, E224, E246, E156). Fathom's own script is a few KB, deferred, CDN-served (E101, E102, E155, E216). Cloudflare's analytics being free is acknowledged in the evidence itself (E126, E125) with no rebuttal on offer — the only counter-argument available is the business-model one (E161, E256).

objections.objection: Nothing is actually broken. Analytics is not this quarter's problem — I'll look at it when I have a spare afternoon.
objections.answer: Answerable only on the history-decay angle, which is genuinely time-sensitive. Google already deleted Universal Analytics data in July 2024 and no importer can recover what Google no longer holds (E65, E94); GA4's standard user- and event-level retention settings are generally 2 or 14 months (E66). So the history that can still be brought over shrinks the longer the decision waits, and once imported it stays viewable and exportable while subscribed (E58, E180, E224). The effort side undercuts the 'spare afternoon' framing: one script tag or an integration (E225, E27, E154, E241), run in parallel with no switch-off required (E239, E193), verified by looking at Realtime (E23). Nothing in the evidence creates an external deadline beyond that, so manufactured urgency would be a lie.

objections.objection: This is a tiny bootstrapped company with two founders. I'm not putting my analytics — or my card — somewhere that could be gone or acquired in two years.
objections.answer: Partly answered, and the evidence cuts both ways, so use it carefully. For durability: independent and bootstrapped with no VC, bank loans or outside shareholders to answer to (E243), a software-not-data business model deliberately priced to be sustainable for a very long time (E201, E242, E257), operating since 2018 (E85), heavy investment in fast reliable infrastructure rather than cheap servers (E200), EU cloud monitored 24/7, highly available and multi-region (E41), built for traffic spikes and large sites (E157). For social proof: used by Fortune 100s, banks and governments (E227, E252), a named logo wall including Microsoft, IBM, GitHub, The New York Times, Laravel, Tailwind, Bosch, HashiCorp (E206, E228), and over a million websites claimed (E226, E209) — note these are vendor statements and logos only, with no usage detail (E130–E137), and a logo does not establish current use. Exit risk is mitigated rather than removed: no contracts, cancel anytime from settings, export your data first, because cancellation queues data for deletion (E194, E92, E151).

profiles.name: Plausible Analytics
profiles.why: Both Plausible and Fathom position themselves as privacy-first, cookieless Google Analytics alternatives with a built-in GA import path—Plausible says 'You can even import your Google Analytics stats' while Fathom's importer requires only authorizing the account, selecting sites and running the import (E74). Plausible markets itself as explicitly EU-hosted, with visitor data processed 'exclusively on servers owned and operated by European companies,' whereas Fathom instead claims its 'intelligent routing' makes its script load 'up to 50% faster than EU-only infrastructure' (E105), treating EU-only hosting as a benchmark to beat rather than a selling point in itself.
profiles.discovery_reason: The closest like-for-like swap buyers compare against when picking a cookieless, EU-friendly analytics tool with a simple dashboard and open-source option.
profiles.one_liner: Easy to use and privacy-friendly Google Analytics alternative
profiles.promise: Plausible is powerful, lightweight analytics. No cookies, just insights. Made and hosted in the EU, powered by European-owned infrastructure.
profiles.pricing: Usage-tiered by monthly pageviews (shown at the 10k tier): Starter $9/month (one site, 3-year retention), Growth $14/month (up to 3 sites, 3 team members), Business $19/month (up to 10 sites, 10 team members, Stats API); Enterprise is custom/contact sales for 10+ sites. Annual billing offers 2 months free versus monthly billing.
profiles.free_entry: 30-day free trial, no credit card required (https://plausible.io/); open-source code available on GitHub.
profiles.icp: Site owners for whom 'Google Analytics is overkill' and who want insights 'without complexity, training or prior analytics experience.'

map.reading:
Assessment summary. Verified quotations do not establish demand or purchase intent; commercial priority remains a hypothesis.
- A technical founder who built the site himself and gave up on GA4 somewhere around the third Explore report: review first; product compatibility supported; audience evidence supported (6 quoted source(s)); use or purchase captured; reachability venue identified.

dossier.orientation: For a solo technical founder who installed their own analytics script, Fathom is a hosted, cookieless website analytics dashboard they add with one line of code and read on a single page, on a paid monthly plan rather than a free tier.

ranked_relevance.why: Documented mechanism: because Fathom uses no cookies, no consent banner is needed, which is the exact burden this audience researched.
States the underlying mechanism ('doesn't even use cookies, ever') that the no-banner consequence rests on.
Documents what the dashboard does — one page, filterable, no months of training — against the researched GA4 complexity.
A single line of code in the header is the installation mechanism for a founder who deploys the site himself and wants minutes, not infrastructure.
Real-time dashboard plus self-verifiable install is the documented behaviour a founder who owns the tag can check himself.
The entry price and pageview allowance are the commercial facts this self-paying buyer decides on; licensed as stated, with no claim of cheapness.
Running alongside existing analytics matches the researched parallel-run migration behaviour of this audience.
Documents the script behaviour (async, not bulky) rather than an opinion about speed.
Saved named filter views describe how the dashboard gets you back to the one number you wanted, the mechanism behind the simplicity fit.
The GA importer is the documented mechanism for keeping GA4 history through a switch.
Documented exception to the importer: supported daily API analytics only, no full report parity and no GA events.
Dated limitation (Google deleted UA data in July 2024) that bounds the importer; it describes that period, not a present trigger.
Retention back to signup, conditional on remaining a customer, is the documented counterpart to history continuity.
No contracts, cancel from settings and export before cancelling lowers the commitment a solo buyer is taking on.
Documented tier-change behaviour with its two-consecutive-month condition, relevant to a founder watching a monthly bill.
Second price point showing how cost scales with pageviews as the site grows.
Describes the GDPR posture (controller/processor, anonymisation, minimisation) behind the no-banner claim and the researched legal anxiety.
Allowed-domain firewall blocking all other hostnames instantly is a documented mechanism for a founder whose local and staging environments share the script.
Handling traffic spikes matches the researched workflow of frequent launch and changelog posts.
Hosted-only with global CDN and EU processing is both the reason there is no infrastructure to run and the documented absence of a self-host option.
Self-described business model (selling software, not data) is the licensed reason the product is paid rather than free.
Customer statement that the dashboard is simple with clear metrics corroborates the simplicity fit but describes an impression, not behaviour.
Ranked only because this audience's self-deployed JS stacks (Next, Nuxt, Vue) appear in its optional stack signal; the wider directory is not established for this buyer.
Duplicate of the same Jessica Joyce quote already licensed as E245; still true, but adds nothing and risks double-citing one voice.
Unqualified 'only choice' superlative flagged weak in the ledger; poor material for a sceptical technical buyer.
Frames the product for governments, enterprises and finance, which is not this solo founder's organisation.
Unverified vendor assertion about Google's motives; the fact stays true as a captured claim but is weak ground for this audience.
Agency client-dashboard allowance addresses an organisation shape this audience does not have (1-10, self-deployed, no clients established).
Background on free privacy-first competitors such as Cloudflare; explains the researched price pressure without licensing any claim.
Background that Matomo's privacy features need setup and knowledge; relevant to the self-hosting overhead complaint but it is a competitor claim, not a product fact.

problem_fits.caveat: The selected evidence describes dashboard behaviour and one customer's impression; no measured outcome shows a GA4 refugee finding answers faster.
problem_fits.why: A single-page filterable dashboard with reopenable saved views is a documented mechanism against the researched 'lost in sub-menu 27' complaint.

problem_fits.caveat: Nothing in the selected evidence quantifies data recovered by dropping a banner, so the researched 30-50% loss cannot be claimed as a Fathom result; whether a site needs a banner for other reasons is not established here.
problem_fits.why: No cookies is a documented mechanism, and the documentation states the direct consequence that no consent banner is needed for analytics.

problem_fits.caveat: The selected evidence establishes real-time display, self-verifiable installation and parallel running, but no accuracy measurement; imported GA4 totals are documented to differ, and this problem rests on a single researched source.
problem_fits.why: The founder can watch his own visit appear and compare against his existing tool, which addresses verifiability without proving the numbers are correct.

problem_fits.caveat: Being hosted-only is the reason there is nothing to run and also means self-hosting or keeping data locally is not available at all; buyers who require that are out of scope.
problem_fits.why: One line of script on a hosted service removes the Docker/Matomo infrastructure the researched founder called disproportionate.

The lowest price licensed by the selected evidence is a paid monthly tier, and no free or lower entry option is established by it, so the researched 'not cheap for an indie developer' objection cannot be answered with a positive product fact.

segment_objections.objection: Free privacy-friendly analytics already exist (Cloudflare, GoatCounter), so why pay a monthly fee at all?
segment_objections.answer: The selected evidence supports only that Fathom's business model is selling software rather than visitor data, that the entry plan is $15/month for up to 100,000 pageviews, and that there are no contracts and cancellation is self-serve; it does not establish that Fathom is cheap for an indie budget.

segment_objections.objection: Do I have to keep a cookie consent banner on my own site?
segment_objections.answer: The documentation states Fathom never uses cookies and that no consent banner is needed for its analytics, and describes anonymisation and data minimisation as its GDPR posture.

segment_objections.objection: If I switch I lose years of Google Analytics history.
segment_objections.answer: The GA importer brings GA4 data into Fathom and history stays viewable while the subscription is active, but it imports only supported daily API analytics, recreates neither every GA4 report nor GA events, and cannot recover Universal Analytics data Google deleted in July 2024.

segment_objections.objection: I want to keep analytics on my own infrastructure, not on a vendor's servers.
segment_objections.answer: Fathom is hosted only; pageviews are processed on a global CDN, EU visitor personal data stays in the EU with anonymised analytics on US infrastructure, and self-hosting is not offered.

segment_objections.objection: Another script on my site will slow down page loads.
segment_objections.answer: The documentation states the small script loads asynchronously so it does not hold up the page, and one customer reports it does not bog down loading times.

segment_objections.objection: Is this going to be another tool I have to learn like GA4?
segment_objections.answer: All data appears on a single page that is filterable without months of training, filter combinations can be saved as named views, and the dashboard is real-time so installation can be checked with one visit.

segment_objections.objection: What happens when a launch post blows past my pageview tier?
segment_objections.answer: Fathom is documented to handle traffic spikes and large sites, and tier changes follow a stated rule: two consecutive months over the limit prompts contact about a larger plan, two consecutive months under allows moving down from billing settings.

silences.reason: The researched complaint is that privacy analytics subscriptions cost more than an indie developer's whole running stack, and the selected evidence offers only paid tiers starting at $15/month with no free or lower-cost option; a free rival is acknowledged in the same material.
silences.question: Does Fathom offer any entry option below $15/month (free tier, low-volume hobby plan, annual discount or student/indie pricing), and is that established anywhere in the full ledger?

silences.reason: Beyond real-time display and parallel running, the selected evidence contains no measurement of counting accuracy, blocker resistance or bot filtering, so the researched 'I don't trust my own dashboard' feeling can only be partly answered.
silences.question: Does the full ledger document how Fathom filters bots and non-human traffic and how its counts compare with another tool on the same site?

research.audience_key: a technical founder who built the site himself and gave up on ga4 somewhere around the third explore report

relevance.audience_name: A technical founder who built the site himself and gave up on GA4 somewhere around the third Explore report

dossier.audience_name: A technical founder who built the site himself and gave up on GA4 somewhere around the third Explore report
dossier.orientation: For a solo technical founder who installed their own analytics script, Fathom is a hosted, cookieless website analytics dashboard they add with one line of code and read on a single page, on a paid monthly plan rather than a free tier.

ranked_relevance.why: Documented mechanism: because Fathom uses no cookies, no consent banner is needed, which is the exact burden this audience researched.
States the underlying mechanism ('doesn't even use cookies, ever') that the no-banner consequence rests on.
Documents what the dashboard does — one page, filterable, no months of training — against the researched GA4 complexity.
A single line of code in the header is the installation mechanism for a founder who deploys the site himself and wants minutes, not infrastructure.
Real-time dashboard plus self-verifiable install is the documented behaviour a founder who owns the tag can check himself.
The entry price and pageview allowance are the commercial facts this self-paying buyer decides on; licensed as stated, with no claim of cheapness.
Running alongside existing analytics matches the researched parallel-run migration behaviour of this audience.
Documents the script behaviour (async, not bulky) rather than an opinion about speed.
Saved named filter views describe how the dashboard gets you back to the one number you wanted, the mechanism behind the simplicity fit.
The GA importer is the documented mechanism for keeping GA4 history through a switch.
Documented exception to the importer: supported daily API analytics only, no full report parity and no GA events.
Dated limitation (Google deleted UA data in July 2024) that bounds the importer; it describes that period, not a present trigger.
Retention back to signup, conditional on remaining a customer, is the documented counterpart to history continuity.
No contracts, cancel from settings and export before cancelling lowers the commitment a solo buyer is taking on.
Documented tier-change behaviour with its two-consecutive-month condition, relevant to a founder watching a monthly bill.
Second price point showing how cost scales with pageviews as the site grows.
Describes the GDPR posture (controller/processor, anonymisation, minimisation) behind the no-banner claim and the researched legal anxiety.
Allowed-domain firewall blocking all other hostnames instantly is a documented mechanism for a founder whose local and staging environments share the script.
Handling traffic spikes matches the researched workflow of frequent launch and changelog posts.
Hosted-only with global CDN and EU processing is both the reason there is no infrastructure to run and the documented absence of a self-host option.
Self-described business model (selling software, not data) is the licensed reason the product is paid rather than free.
Customer statement that the dashboard is simple with clear metrics corroborates the simplicity fit but describes an impression, not behaviour.
Ranked only because this audience's self-deployed JS stacks (Next, Nuxt, Vue) appear in its optional stack signal; the wider directory is not established for this buyer.
Duplicate of the same Jessica Joyce quote already licensed as E245; still true, but adds nothing and risks double-citing one voice.
Unqualified 'only choice' superlative flagged weak in the ledger; poor material for a sceptical technical buyer.
Frames the product for governments, enterprises and finance, which is not this solo founder's organisation.
Unverified vendor assertion about Google's motives; the fact stays true as a captured claim but is weak ground for this audience.
Agency client-dashboard allowance addresses an organisation shape this audience does not have (1-10, self-deployed, no clients established).
Background on free privacy-first competitors such as Cloudflare; explains the researched price pressure without licensing any claim.
Background that Matomo's privacy features need setup and knowledge; relevant to the self-hosting overhead complaint but it is a competitor claim, not a product fact.

problem_fits.caveat: The selected evidence describes dashboard behaviour and one customer's impression; no measured outcome shows a GA4 refugee finding answers faster.
problem_fits.why: A single-page filterable dashboard with reopenable saved views is a documented mechanism against the researched 'lost in sub-menu 27' complaint.

problem_fits.caveat: Nothing in the selected evidence quantifies data recovered by dropping a banner, so the researched 30-50% loss cannot be claimed as a Fathom result; whether a site needs a banner for other reasons is not established here.
problem_fits.why: No cookies is a documented mechanism, and the documentation states the direct consequence that no consent banner is needed for analytics.

problem_fits.caveat: The selected evidence establishes real-time display, self-verifiable installation and parallel running, but no accuracy measurement; imported GA4 totals are documented to differ, and this problem rests on a single researched source.
problem_fits.why: The founder can watch his own visit appear and compare against his existing tool, which addresses verifiability without proving the numbers are correct.

problem_fits.caveat: Being hosted-only is the reason there is nothing to run and also means self-hosting or keeping data locally is not available at all; buyers who require that are out of scope.
problem_fits.why: One line of script on a hosted service removes the Docker/Matomo infrastructure the researched founder called disproportionate.

The lowest price licensed by the selected evidence is a paid monthly tier, and no free or lower entry option is established by it, so the researched 'not cheap for an indie developer' objection cannot be answered with a positive product fact.

segment_objections.objection: Free privacy-friendly analytics already exist (Cloudflare, GoatCounter), so why pay a monthly fee at all?
segment_objections.answer: The selected evidence supports only that Fathom's business model is selling software rather than visitor data, that the entry plan is $15/month for up to 100,000 pageviews, and that there are no contracts and cancellation is self-serve; it does not establish that Fathom is cheap for an indie budget.

segment_objections.objection: Do I have to keep a cookie consent banner on my own site?
segment_objections.answer: The documentation states Fathom never uses cookies and that no consent banner is needed for its analytics, and describes anonymisation and data minimisation as its GDPR posture.

segment_objections.objection: If I switch I lose years of Google Analytics history.
segment_objections.answer: The GA importer brings GA4 data into Fathom and history stays viewable while the subscription is active, but it imports only supported daily API analytics, recreates neither every GA4 report nor GA events, and cannot recover Universal Analytics data Google deleted in July 2024.

segment_objections.objection: I want to keep analytics on my own infrastructure, not on a vendor's servers.
segment_objections.answer: Fathom is hosted only; pageviews are processed on a global CDN, EU visitor personal data stays in the EU with anonymised analytics on US infrastructure, and self-hosting is not offered.

segment_objections.objection: Another script on my site will slow down page loads.
segment_objections.answer: The documentation states the small script loads asynchronously so it does not hold up the page, and one customer reports it does not bog down loading times.

segment_objections.objection: Is this going to be another tool I have to learn like GA4?
segment_objections.answer: All data appears on a single page that is filterable without months of training, filter combinations can be saved as named views, and the dashboard is real-time so installation can be checked with one visit.

segment_objections.objection: What happens when a launch post blows past my pageview tier?
segment_objections.answer: Fathom is documented to handle traffic spikes and large sites, and tier changes follow a stated rule: two consecutive months over the limit prompts contact about a larger plan, two consecutive months under allows moving down from billing settings.
